🇷🇺 🛢 Russian Oil Fetches Premium Prices as Gulf Supplies Tighten China and India are on track to buy record volumes of Russian crude in 2026, and some refiners paid a premium to secure it. With oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted, buyers who once counted on a discount for Russian barrels found themselves bidding against each other for cargoes that could reach their ports. On August 17, Russia’s Urals crude was priced $3.20 a barrel below the Brent benchmark for delivery to India’s west coast. By September 14, it was $1.05 above, according to Platts. That same day, Urals still traded at a discount of nearly $22 at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk. The premium showed what Indian refiners would pay to get oil to their door. The price at the Russian dock told a different story. In China, the bidding went higher. In September, sellers were asking more than $20 above Brent for November deliveries of ESPO, the Russian crude shipped from the Pacific coast, to Shandong province. A tanker loading in Russia’s Far East can reach a Chinese refinery without passing through Hormuz. When Gulf shipments became unreliable, that route gave Russian suppliers room to ask for more. Chinese customs figures show how far refiners changed their buying habits. China’s total crude imports fell 15% in the first ten months of the year, yet its purchases from Russia rose 17%. Russia supplied roughly one in four barrels China imported. In India, Russian crude accounted for 38% of imports over the same period. Russia had extra crude to sell because drone strikes and repairs forced some of its refineries to cut back. Oil those plants would normally turn into diesel and other fuels went overseas as crude. Temporary US sanctions waivers also gave Asian buyers access to more tankers and suppliers as Washington sought to keep oil flowing. Russia’s pricing power now depends in part on how much Gulf oil makes it back to market. Indian refiners expect to scale back their Russian purchases if Middle Eastern deliveries return to normal. Until then, a Russian supplier with a cargo ready to ship can ask a higher price from a refinery that needs to know when its next tanker will arrive. @NewRulesGeo ❗ Follow us on X
